#7741. Airbnb Just Did Something Guests Have Been Asking for Years — Here’s What Changed

Airbnb is putting limits on checkout chores, including washing dishes and stripping beds. Here's what hosts can still ask guests to do.

Everyone loves a vacation. But the cleanup and tidying as the trip is finishing up? Not so much.

It’s not always clear what guests are responsible for cleaning. Dishes, sheets, towels, and taking out the trash are sometimes part of checkout instructions at Airbnb rentals. With checkout typically at 11 a.m., the last morning of a trip can turn into a mad dash through an unreasonably long chore list, even when a cleaning fee has been tacked onto the bill.

That frustration, along with a growing number of travelers returning to hotels for more consistent quality and fees, is behind Airbnb’s new checkout rules. Learn which tasks guests may still face, and how hosts are responding.

Starting with reservations booked on or after November 20, 2026, Airbnb will require hosts to clearly explain their house rules and checkout requests before guests book. Hosts won’t be allowed to add new requirements through messages or signs inside the rental after a reservation is confirmed.

“House Rules are now displayed more prominently on your listing, where guests can easily see them before they book,” according to Airbnb’s announcement. Guests can also find these instructions in their Trips tab and reservation reminders.

Under the new policy, hosts generally can’t require guests to strip beds, start laundry, wash and put away dishes, or take trash to an off-site disposal facility. However, hosts can still request simpler tasks, such as placing dirty dishes in the sink, gathering used towels, or putting trash and recycling in designated bins. Guests may also be asked to turn off lights and return keys before leaving.

Airbnb’s policy distinguishes between house rules and requests. “Guests must follow hosts’ house rules, and are encouraged to comply with hosts’ requests,” according to the company. Some exceptions may apply. For example, rentals in areas with bears may require guests to use animal-proof trash containers, while drought restrictions could affect water use.

Guests are still responsible for leaving the property reasonably tidy. Airbnb’s ground rules for guests prohibit excessive messes and require guests to take responsibility for damage beyond normal wear and tear. Hosts can still charge standard cleaning fees and request reimbursement for unexpected cleaning costs or damage.

Hosts who don’t follow Airbnb’s new checkout rules could receive warnings or requests to update their listings. Repeated violations may lead to notices on their listings or lower placement in search results. Hosts can also appeal flagged requests.

The policy also prevents hosts from charging their own fines for missed chores or restricting access to amenities already included in a reservation.

However, not every host supports the changes. Some believe washing dishes after cooking is a reasonable responsibility for guests, while others worry the new rules could increase cleaning costs. A Change.org petition has called on Airbnb to reverse its restrictions on requiring guests to wash dishes.

Guests who encounter unexpected chores or requests that violate the new policy can contact Airbnb for help.

#7740. City's Using Meta Moderation Assist Feature for Facebook Comments Doesn't Violate First Amendment

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Judge Ruth Bermudez Montenegro (S.D. Cal.) Oct. 22 in Jalisi v. City of Poway:

The City of Poway … maintains a public Facebook page where it "posts updates about various items that may be of interest to [City] residents and the general public." The Facebook page is open to public comment, and members of the public routinely comment on posts on the page. Plaintiff is a resident of Poway who has criticized aspects of the City's decisions for several years, including by speaking during city council meetings, corresponding with City officials, and posting critical comments on the City's Facebook page. City officials and staff, including those responsible for the Facebook page, appear to recognize Plaintiff as a critic.

Several times during the past year, Plaintiff's comments on the City's Facebook page have been "hidden" or "shadow banned;" that is, his comments are not deleted and are still visible when Plaintiff looks at the posts, but are not visible when other Facebook users look at the posts. The City's Social Media Policy provides that "[t]he City's social media presence serves as a limited public forum and all content shall be monitored and moderated." The Policy indicates that user-generated posts will be deleted if those posts, among other things: "use[ ] abusive, vulgar, offensive, profane, sexual, threatening, deliberately untruthful or defamatory language or content." Additionally, "[p]ostings from a public user account which contain inappropriate or disruptive content, … or believed to be spam, may result in the public user account being blocked from any further activity on the City's social media account … at the discretion of the City Manager's Office."

Plaintiff believes that the City is hiding his comments because it wants to suppress his critical viewpoints…. The City represents that none of its employees have ever hidden or removed any comments made by Plaintiff; instead, Meta's Moderation Assist Program has hidden these comments because it has flagged Plaintiff's Facebook profile as a "non-human 'bot'" account. Meta Moderation Assist "is necessary because the City does not have the resources nor ability to actively monitor each and every comment made in real time in order to manually hide bot comments, particularly considering these comments can be submitted 24 hours a day seven days a week." The City believes that Plaintiff's comments were hidden because Moderation Assist flagged him as a bot: "Moderation Assist will automatically hide a post if (1) the commenter does not have any friends or followers, (2) the comment has a link, or (3) the commenter does not have a profile picture." Plaintiff does not have a profile picture, has only one Facebook friend, and has no posts on his own profile, which "are typically strong indicators that the account is a non-human bot."

The city agreed that viewpoint-based moderation of Jalisi's posts would be unconstitutional, and agreed to "… manually unhiding Plaintiff's prior Facebook posts." But it opposed Plaintiff's request to "remove any restriction that causes Plaintiff's comments on the City Page to be hidden from the public"; it argued that it needed to keep using the Moderation Assist program, and couldn't turn it off only for Jalisi. And the court held in favor of the city as to this:

[T]he Court need decide whether the City's Facebook page is a limited public forum or a designated public forum. Even when considering laws regulating expression in "quintessential public forums," courts "ask first whether the law is content based or content neutral." …

As a threshold matter, based on the limited and preliminary record before it, the Court notes it is likely that Plaintiff's comments were hidden not by a City policy, but by the Meta Moderation Assist Program. But even assuming … that the restrictive effects of the Meta Moderation Assist Program may be attributed to the City, the Court does not find the restrictions unconstitutional.

First, the restriction is facially content neutral. Based on the Carmichael Declaration, profiles are not flagged as bots by "examin[ing] the content of the message that is conveyed." Rather, they are flagged based on the presence of certain predictive factors, such as the absence of a profile picture or the absence of other Facebook friends. Thus, determining whether a comment may be hidden has nothing to do with the content of the comment.

Second, the restriction can be "justified without reference to the content of the regulated speech" and there is no sign that the restriction was "adopted by the government because of disagreement with the message [the speech] conveys." The City uses Meta Moderation Assist because it "does not have the resources nor ability to actively monitor each and every comment made in real time in order to manually hide bot comments." There is nothing in the record to suggest that the City turned to Meta Moderation Assist "motivated by disagreement with any particular expressive" conduct. Indeed, Plaintiff's evidence that identical comments published by other users remained visible actually strengthens the finding that the restriction is content neutral; critical speech is clearly tolerated by the City. Therefore, the Court finds that the restriction is content neutral and applies intermediate scrutiny.

To survive intermediate scrutiny, the restriction must "'further[ ] an important or substantial governmental interest,' that interest must be 'unrelated to the suppression of free expression,' and the 'incidental restriction on alleged First Amendment freedoms [must be] no greater than is essential to the furtherance of that interest.'"

The City asserts that its interest in using Meta Moderation Assist is "prevent[ing] non-human 'bot' spam postings on its Facebook page, which can overwhelm public pages and make it much more difficult for the public to both obtain important information and participate in the conversation." The Court finds that the two-way exchange of information between the citizenry and the City is a substantial governmental interest.

Furthermore, that interest is "unrelated to the suppression of free expression." In fact, the interest runs counter to the suppression of free expression; it seeks to ensure that residents have effective access to the exchange of ideas with their neighbors and their government. The interest is related to the suppression of expression by non-human bots, but bots are neither "human beings with First Amendment rights" nor the "[corporations] … composed of [them … that] possess First Amendment rights themselves."

Finally, although the record shows there are "incidental restriction[s]" on speech, such as the hiding of comments posted by human beings flagged as bots, those "incidental restriction[s]" are "no greater than essential to the furtherance" of the governmental interest here. "A critical feature of this inquiry turns on whether the [government] seriously undertook to address the problems it faces with less intrusive tools readily available to it." Again, on the early record before it, the Court finds that the City has no alternative methods to prevent non-human bot accounts from flooding their Facebook page. This is not a situation where there is an obvious, alternative method of regulation that would achieve the governmental interest and incidentally censor no speech….

Alan B. Fenstermacher and Jayson A. Parsons (Rutan & Tucker) represent the City.

#7738. How Does Google Maps Know There’s Traffic Before You Hit It?

A map app can spot a traffic jam before drivers reach it. Here’s how phones detect slowdowns, predict delays, and sometimes get it wrong.

Most drivers know this experience. They’re en route somewhere when their smartphone map app starts pushing back their ETA. Soon, brake lights appear ahead as traffic slows to a crawl.

But how did the navigation app know about the traffic before the driver encountered it? Popular navigation apps like Google Maps, Apple Maps, and Waze use real-time location data from drivers’ phones to detect slowdowns and estimate traffic conditions.

Learn what’s happening and why the estimates aren’t always right.

Map apps combine location data from many phones to understand traffic conditions on the road. Google explains that it uses combined location data for this, and Waze says drivers share real-time information just by driving with the app open. When enough drivers slow down in the same area, the app can show a backup on the map.

Apps also use past traffic information to predict delays before drivers encounter them. “To predict what traffic will look like in the near future, Google Maps analyzes historical traffic patterns for roads over time,” Google’s wevsite states.

These predictions help apps estimate arrival times and suggest alternate routes when traffic starts building.

“Our predictive traffic models are also a key part of how Google Maps determines driving routes,” the Google website continues. “If we predict that traffic is likely to become heavy in one direction, we’ll automatically find you a lower-traffic alternative. We also look at a number of other factors, like road quality. Is the road paved or unpaved, or covered in gravel, dirt or mud?”

Drivers can also report problems such as accidents and hazards through Google Maps, Apple Maps, and Waze, though the options vary by app and region. These reports help explain why traffic has slowed down. Google says it also uses data from local governments, which can flag road restrictions such as construction.

The colored lines on the map show where traffic is building. In most navigational systems, green means no traffic delays, orange means medium traffic, and red means delays, with darker red indicating slower speeds.

Traffic updates are generally useful, but they aren’t always accurate. Apple, for example, says it displays incident markers only when it has a high level of confidence in the reports it receives, so a new incident may take time to appear. Coverage also varies depending on how much information the apps receive. On less-traveled roads, fewer drivers may contribute location data, making it harder for apps to detect slowdowns in real time.

Arrival times are estimates, too. Google says its predictions combine historical patterns with live conditions, but it also notes that historical patterns aren’t always reliable indicators of what the road will look like. Conditions can also change unexpectedly because of events like snowstorms.

Map apps can help drivers avoid delays, but their estimates aren’t guaranteed. Drivers still need to follow road signs and pay attention to the conditions around them.

#7737. Don’t Get Caught Off Guard by the First Frost Again — Bookmark This Checklist for Next Year

From HVAC systems to roofs and paint cans, these simple maintenance tasks can prevent big-ticket repairs.

In years past, when I’ve failed to prep my home for the first frost, I’ve ended up with burst garden hoses, broken tree limbs and cars that won’t start. But sometimes, procrastinating on winterizing a home can lead to even more severe problems, including foundation damage and burst pipes.

“If you want to save money and protect your pocket book, then jump on the winterization of your home and yard,” says home improvement expert Todd Tripp. “Before the first frost is also an excellent time to put your yard and equipment to sleep, so that it will start fresh for you in the spring.”

Ahead, Tripp and other experts walk through exactly what to do before the first frost of the season.

Water that accumulates around a home during winter can cause foundation damage as it freezes and thaws. Before the first frost comes, clean leaves and other debris from the gutters and downspouts, check for leaks and extend downspouts so they carry water at least 10 feet away from the house.

Common mistake: “Don’t clean the gutters too early in the fall, before nearby trees have finished shedding their leaves,” says remodeling expert Michael DiMartino.

Many outdoor water systems fall victim to the first freeze, bursting as the water inside of them expands into ice. To prevent this:

“It’s also a good idea to put the hoses and other garden equipment in a shed, so they’re covered and out of the elements,” says Tripp.

Freezing water can split plumbing pipes. Then, once temperatures rise, the water leaking out can cause significant damage. To prevent this, use foam insulation sleeves, insulation tape or heat tape around pipes that run through unheated areas, such as garages, crawls spaces, basements, attics and exterior walls.

“Also, look for gaps around windows, doors, foundations and where pipes enter the home, and seal them properly, since cold drafts can make vulnerable plumbing even more susceptible to freezing,” says plumber Tim Fancher. As a bonus, this will also help keep mice and spiders out.

Pro-tip: know where your main water shutoff is, says Fancher. If a pipe does burst, quickly shutting off the water will help mitigate damage.

Frost can cause weak trees limbs to fall, potentially damaging your roof or car, so trim trees before the winter season begins. That will also keep dead leaves from accumulating on your roof.

While you’re at it, prune shrubbery and cut back perennial plants. “Before the frost comes is also a good time to put in your winter fertilizer,” says Tripp. “Blend on your lawn and in your flowerbeds so that it will percolate down into the soil over the winter.”

Cracks or damaged seals can let in moisture, which will cause further damage, plus invite cold drafts. Before the first frost, caulk any gaps and fix damaged weather stripping. “This will also save you a lot of money on your heating bill, plus keep moisture and mold out of your house,” says Tripp.

Also, fogging between your window panes is often a sign that the window seal has failed, and the window may not be insulating your house as well as it once did, says DiMartino.

Any damage to your roof will likely get worse once temperatures drop. Before the first frost, visually inspect your roof for missing, loose or damaged shingles and signs of water intrusion. Also, check the attic for moisture.

Pro-tip: “If you notice moisture in the attic or leaks in the home’s living spaces, it could be a sign that the roof needs to be repaired or replaced,” says DiMartino.

A freezing evening is no time to have the furnace fail. That could lead to burst pipes and even jeopardize your family’s safety. Home improvement expert Eric Goranson recommends hiring a pro to inspect your system every year, plus tune it for maximum efficiency.

While you’re at it, don’t forget to winterize your air conditioning system. “It’s not completely necessary to cover the outside condenser unit, but it’s a good practice to cover it or wrap it to protect it from frost,” says Tripp.

Safety check: Before using your furnace or fireplace in the fall, check your chimney for debris like spiderwebs and bird nests, which could cause it to not vent properly, or even catch on fire.

Cold weather can reduce your battery’s cold cranking amps, making it hard to start on the first cold morning, says Goranson. Before the first frost, test your battery, check your tires and windshield wipers and bring other neglected maintenance up to date.

Pro-tip: Run a Top Tier fuel through your vehicle at least once a month. “Those have cleaners in them that help keep your engine’s fuel system clean,” says Goranson.

Drain fuel or put fuel stabilizers in gas-powered lawnmowers, trimmers and blowers, before stowing them in the shed. “The best trick I was ever told, which has worked for over 30 years, is to drain the fuel out of your landscape equipment, then start it up and let it run until it’s completely out of gas,” says Tripp. “That gets all the fuel out of your carburetor so that it does not varnish or gum up, and it will start in the spring every time.”

For electric-powered equipment, charge the batteries to the manufacturer-recommended levels, then leave them in a temperature-controlled space.

If your garage isn’t insulated, chances are there are items in there that won’t fare well when temperatures drop. Especially check the storage instructions on paints and other liquids, plus battery-powered equipment. Also, don’t forget to check the seals on your garage door.

Pro-tip: Move shovels and ice melt to a place where they’re easy to access, leave a clear walking path through the garage and designate somewhere to put wet boots and tools, says garage expert Alan Bernau Jr. “You want to be able to use the garage in winter, not just cram everything into it,” he says.

#7735. If You Spot OTR on a Truck, Here’s What It Means

Those three letters on a semi-truck usually refer to long-distance driving. Learn what OTR means and how different trucking routes work.

Trucks are full of weird and useful features that most people overlook without knowing their real purpose. Some have long spikes on their wheels. Others might feature amber lights on top. You might even see diamond shaped signs. But what about OTR written on a truck?

What can look like a government code can have a specific meaning in the trucking industry. Learn what OTR means, how long-haul work compares with shorter routes, and why the context matters.

In trucking, OTR stands for “over-the-road.” It refers to long-haul trucking, where drivers transport freight across long distances, often through several states or into Canada. According to trucking company Schneider, OTR drivers can spend weeks away from home. Many drive trucks with sleeper cabs that provide a place to rest between shifts.

OTR describes the type of work, not a specific truck. It’s also not a required marking. The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) requires certain identifying information, including a company’s name and USDOT number, on interstate commercial trucks, but OTR isn’t part of that requirement.

The letters can also mean something different depending on where they appear. In the tire industry, OTR stands for “off-the-road,” referring to heavy-duty tires used on construction and mining equipment. OTR Diagnostics is also the name of a maintenance tool that helps truck owners check engine problems and other vehicle information.

OTR truck drivers transport freight over long distances, often making several stops along the way. Their jobs can also involve inspecting their trucks, handling delivery paperwork, and sometimes helping load or unload cargo.

Because these trips can last for weeks, drivers often sleep in their trucks or stop at other places along their routes. The FMCSA limits how long commercial drivers can drive without taking required breaks and rest periods.

Drivers who operate most full-size tractor-trailers need a Class A commercial driver’s license (CDL). Depending on the company and route, drivers may spend several weeks working before returning home.

OTR drivers cover the longest distances and may spend weeks away from home. Regional drivers work within a particular area of the country, often returning home weekly or more frequently. Local drivers generally stay closer to home and return after each shift, although they can still work long hours.

There’s also dedicated trucking, where drivers regularly transport freight for the same customer or between the same locations. These routes can be local, regional, or long-distance, depending on the company.

The exact distances and schedules vary between employers, so the terms don’t always describe the same mileage or amount of time away from home.

Schneider, “Over-the-Road (OTR) Truck Driving Jobs” Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration, “How Do I Get a Commercial Driver’s License?” OTR Performance, “Why Choose OTR Diagnostics?“

#7734. Is a Reverse Osmosis Filter System Actually Worth It? We Break Down Every Cost

What’s lurking in your water? RO filters get rid of everything from microplastics to heavy metals, but are they overkill?

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

In this installment of Home 2.0, we dive into reverse osmosis filtration for the kitchen, its benefits and hidden costs — plus which households should invest in the technology, and who can skip it.

I’ve lived in some places with questionable drinking water. One town issued a notice that the municipal water supply had experienced a sewage incident. Another had an arsenic problem. I’ve also lived on well water, with concerns of contamination from nearby agricultural fields.

My solution used to be buying five-gallon jugs of spring water. But that was costly and a hassle, so six years ago, I switched to an under-sink reverse osmosis (RO) filter for my drinking and cooking water.

Under-sink RO filters work like this: water passes through a series of filters, including an RO membrane, which removes dissolved substances — including lead, arsenic, nitrates, forever chemicals, chlorine, fluoride and sediment — down to 0.0001 microns. The cleaned water then comes out through a faucet, installed near the sink.

“Reverse osmosis provides the safest level of drinking water possible,” says international water filtration specialist Andrew D. Daily. “It strips out 100% of bacteria, cysts, dissolved solids, chlorine, rust, viruses and microplastics.”

But RO systems are also a considerable investment. So, we asked a range of health and plumbing experts for their thoughts on who should get an RO system, plus how to pick the right one. Ahead is what they said, how much RO systems cost up front and over time, and whether it’s worth the upgrade.

RO water systems range from a few hundred dollars to over $1,000. The good news is that if you have basic plumbing knowledge and are comfortable drilling a hole in your countertop, installing one can be a DIY task. Otherwise, pro installation usually runs upwards of $300, not including add-ons like a refrigerator/ice-maker connection, leak protection, an additional electric outlet and other plumbing modifications.

The biggest downside to RO systems is that they waste water. For every gallon that comes out of the faucet, somewhere between one-half and four gallons get flushed down the drain through the filtration process. That means if you use 5 gallons of water a day for cooking and drinking, the RO system wastes between 2.5 and 20 gallons.

Over a year, that adds up to between 500 and 8,500 gallons, depending on your RO system. On the low end, that’s only a few pennies more on your yearly water utility bill, but on the high end, it could be close to $100.

Some RO water systems also require electricity. The amount of power they consume varies by model, but usually falls between 20 and 40 watts per hour. Since RO systems typically run for less than an hour a day, even if you live in a place with high electricity rates, they should add only a few dollars a year to your electricity bill.

Maintaining RO systems is an easy DIY task, though some people choose to pay a pro to keep track of it for them. Expect to spend roughly the following for DIY maintenance:

Daily recommends buying only name-brand filters, even though they’re more expensive. “Name brands follow strict regulations,” he says. ”Generic China-based deals often do not provide the same protection.”

A quality RO system can last 10 years or longer with proper maintenance. “Many parts, including filters, membranes, faucets and tanks can be replaced individually,” says plumbing expert Danielle Smith. “Once a system gets older, though, replacement may make more sense than repeated repairs.”

“The biggest thing for me is convenience,” says environmental and wellness expert Helen Christoni, who has an AquaTru system. “We use water all day long, drinking it, cooking with it and filling water bottles. Once installed, it just became part of my kitchen and my family’s daily health.”

Herman Hartanto, founder of Tampa Fast Home Buyer, has a Waterdrop G3P600 in his kitchen ($429 retail). It’s a tankless model, a feature he appreciates since it takes up minimal cabinet space. He also likes the display with real-time reports on total dissolved solids (TDS) and filter health. His only complaint is the occasional noise it generates. “The pump that draws the water on demand makes quite loud noise, which I can feel clearly at night when everything is silent,” he says.

Personally, I’ve used two RO filter systems. My first one was an iSpring, which I chose because of its affordability. It worked well, but like Hartanto, I found the pump noisy (even though mine had a water-holding tank). My second one, which I’ve only recently installed, is a Waterdrop X12 Pro, which I chose to upgrade to because of its water-saving efficiency, ability to add calcium and magnesium back into the water, clear display and range of other premium features. So far, I’ve found it to be quiet, efficient, and free of quirks (though at $1,400 off-sale, the price is a bit of a shocker).

Depending on what type of contaminants you have in your water, there are several alternatives to an under-sink RO water filter:

“Find out what’s in your water before buying anything,” says Smith. “Don’t choose a system based only on how many stages it has or how many contaminants the box says it removes. Instead, start with your water and choose the system around what you actually need.”

If you’re worried about contaminants like microplastics, arsenic, lead, forever chemicals, pesticides and pharmaceuticals, then an RO filter is a good choice.

“Water quality can vary tremendously depending on where you live, and even your home’s plumbing can affect what ultimately comes out of your faucet,” says Christoni. “Reverse osmosis addresses such a broad range of contaminants, and with an under-sink system, that purified water is available all day long without having to think about it.”

For Daily, the biggest reason to invest in a RO system is microplastics. “The amount of microplastics found in human brains, blood and organs have been increasing yearly,” he says. “Although there is not enough information to prove a detrimental effect on our health, many of my clients choose a cautious approach to water treatment.”

Otherwise, Daily says that RO filters are overkill in most U.S. cities, where tap water is generally considered safe. Even in Mexico, where water is often contaminated, he usually recommends sticking with under-sink ultrafiltration systems, since they’re a fraction of the cost, don’t waste water and don’t require power or space for a reservoir.

If you’re currently buying bottled water, then yes, an RO system will soon pay for itself. But, otherwise, it really just depends on what you want to remove from your water. If you have arsenic, nitrates, salts, microplastics, fluoride, sulfates and other dissolved solids (TDS), RO systems are a great solution.

Otherwise, a less-expensive ultrafiltration system might be a better choice. Either way, having an under-sink filtration system is a good way to ensure your family has access to clean water, both on a daily basis and after flooding events and other natural disasters that contaminate city and well water.

#7732. Accusing University Lecturer Who Called Police of "Blatant Racial Profiling" Leads to $37,500 Defamation Verdict

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

You can see the verdict form, from Thursday, here. The jury had asked whether they could suggest additional remedies besides the money:

But the court referred the jury to Instruction No. 10, which focused solely on monetary damages.

The backstory, from the opinion this April Judge Rebecca Pennell (E.D. Wash.) in Riera v. Central Wash. Univ., which let the case go forward:

Mr. Riera was employed in a fixed term, non-tenure track faculty at Central Washington University (CWU)…. On the morning of April 1, [2024,] Mr. Riera called the CWU police to report an older, "apparently homeless," woman wandering around Samuelson Hall. He said he wanted to make a report "before things get … out of control." An officer reported to Samuelson Hall and confirmed the identity of the woman as a CWU professor. No further action was taken by campus police or Mr. Riera.

The CWU professor shared her experience with two colleagues. The colleagues immediately filed bias complaints with CWU, alleging the target of Mr. Riera's call—a Black woman—had been the victim of racial profiling.

This led to a great deal of institutional response, including a discussion at a faculty senate meeting. Defendant Erdman, "a lecturer at CWU and member of the faculty senate, emailed unofficial minutes [of the meeting] to non-tenured faculty," and her notes included this:

Without naming names or describing the incident, [CWU President] Wohlpart expressed his outrage at a recent unconscionable incident on campus.

From my own knowledge, I think I can tell you the basics: It was an incident of blatant racial profiling. Campus police were called because a person of color was sitting quietly in the lobby of a CWU building for a brief interval. The person turned out to be a highly distinguished faculty member—but was compelled to produce and show ID before being left in peace.

(I must remark that this is outrageous on multiple levels. All CWU buildings are public; they belong to the State of Washington and its people. Anyone may sit in the lobby of any of our buildings. There was no reason at all to call the police—except, I guess, that this was a person of color.)

Wohlpart called the incident "unacceptable" and said that Central is working to see to it that such a thing doesn't happen again on our campus….

Riera sued Erdman, among others, and the court allowed his defamation claim to go forward in part:

[M]ost of [Erdman's] statements cannot be characterized as false. The only exception is Defendant Erdman's statement that what happened on April 1 "was an incident of blatant racial profiling." A jury could conclude this statement falsely asserts that the person who called police on April 1 engaged in intentional racial profiling. And, given widely-shared public records revealed Mr. Riera as the caller, a jury could also conclude Defendant Erdman's statement was about Mr. Riera.

Defendants argue that regardless of truth or falsity, Defendant Erdman's statement cannot be considered defamatory because it falls under the common interest privilege. "The common interest privilege applies with the declarant and the recipient have a common interest in the subject matter of the communication." The privilege applies to "persons involved in the same organization, partnerships, associations, or enterprises who are communicating on matters of common interest." Examples include officers of a nonprofit association or partners to a partnership. The privilege arises "when parties need to speak freely and openly about subjects of common organizational or pecuniary interest." …

If the privilege exists, it can be lost in two circumstances (1) if the speaker is not acting in the ordinary course of their work or (2) the speaker's statement was made with actual malice; i.e., reckless disregard for the truth. Whether the privilege has been lost under either scenario is a question of fact.

Here, the parties appear to agree that members of CWU's faculty senate are members of the same organization who share a common interest. The dispute lies in whether an exception applies.

The Court concludes there are issues of fact regarding whether Defendant Erdman's statements fell outside the scope of the privilege. Going to the first exception, Defendant Erdman had no official responsibility for taking notes at faculty meetings and she was not required to share her notes with other members of the senate faculty. A jury could therefore conclude that her statements were outside the ordinary course of her work as a member of a senate.

With respect to the second exception, Defendant Erdman was not a witness to the April 1 incident and no investigation had yet taken place. A jury could therefore conclude Defendant Erdman was reckless in asserting that the call to CWU police was an act of blatant racial profiling…. [T]he allegations against Defendant Erdman raise questions of fact that must be resolved by a jury.

Note that the court granted summary judgment as to plaintiff's defamation claim against President Wohlpart; as to plaintiff's defamation claim against CWU, the court stated that "Mr. Riera appears to have abandoned this claim and the summary judgment briefing does not describe how CWU as an institution may be liable for defamation." The one remaining defendant at trial was Erdman.

UPDATE 11/3/26 4:45 pm: I had originally written that the claims against the University were abandoned, but apparently plaintiff's counsel is disputing that, and intends to appeal the court's dismissal of the claims against CWU and Wohlpart. I've revised the post to say that the court stated the claim was abandoned.

#7731. Step Up Your Game With a DIY Folding Step Stool

This weekend project walks you through every cut and joint to make a foldable step stool you’ll actually use every day.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Turn leftover hardwood scraps into a rock-solid folding step stool that puts wobbly plastic versions to shame.

At some point in our lives we will need a folding step stool. You know, the one that stays out of the way but, gives you that little extra boost when you don’t need a full step ladder. In my case, I find myself reaching for a step stool more often than I’d like to admit especially when trying to reach into a work truck. When I need something, I prefer to make it and am happy to share the steps with you. Just because it is small doesn’t mean it isn’t as satisfying to make – enjoy!

On the miter saw and/or table saw, cut the top step (A), all four legs (B), the guides (C), ad the bottom crossbrace (E). Set aside everything but the legs (B) until later.

Using a compass with a pencil, draw 1-1/2-inch diameter half-circles at the bottom of each leg (B) to match the 1/2-inch width of the leg.

Use a disc or belt sander with a coarse-grit sandpaper (80 or 100-grit) to shape the ends of the legs by sanding up to the marked pencil lines for your arch. Once you have sanded to the line, work your way up to 220-grit sandpaper for a smoother finish.

Using a router table or a router equipped with a 1/4-inch round-over bit, round over all the edges of the step (A) and all four legs (B). Be sure to use clamps to hold the pieces while making your passes with the router.

With all the parts machined, sand all the components to 220 grit and apply a couple of coats of a wood finish of your choice. Allow the finish to dry before moving on to assembly.

Spread wood glue in hole 3 at the top of each inside leg (B). Insert the ends of the 3/4-in. dowel cross brace (D) and tap the legs on with a rubber mallet until D is fully seated.

Set the 1-1/4-in.-square cross brace (E) between the bottoms of the legs, with its bottom edge 2-1/8 in. up from the bottom of the legs. To keep the legs parallel while you drill, clamp a scrap the same length as the cross brace (E) between them at mid-height. Check for square.

Using hole 4 in each leg as a guide, drill a 1/2-in. hole about 1 in. deep into the center of each end of the cross brace (E). Glue 1/2-in. dowels, cut longer than the holes are deep, and drive them through the legs with a mallet until they bottom out in the cross brace (E).

Lock each of the four joints with a single brad nail through the leg into the dowel. Trim the protruding ends of all the dowels flush with a pull saw.

Flip the top step (A) upside down. Position the guide rails (C) 1/2-in. in from each side and centered front to back, leaving 1-1/2-in. at the front and back. Trace around each rail.

Drill two 1/4-in. holes, 3/4-in. deep, centered on each outline. Keep the bit plumb when drilling (or drill at the drill press).

Insert dowel centers in the holes. Align each rail with its outline and press down to mark the hole locations. Drill matching 1/4-in. holes in the rails, about 7/8-in. deep. That’s slightly deeper than the dowel needs, which leaves room for glue.

Glue and insert 1/4-in x 1-1/2-in. dowels and secure the guide rails (C) to the step (A).

Thread 1/4-inch x 3-1/2-inch carriage bolts through hole 1 in the center of the legs to connect an outside leg to the outside of each of the connected inside legs. Put a washer between each pair of legs and secure with a nylon lock nut on the inside of the inside legs.

Connect the two outside legs (B) to the sides of the guide rails (C) by threading 1/4-inch x 2-1/2-inch pan head screws through hole 5 in the guide rails and through hole 2 on the outside legs. Use a washer on the outside of the guide rails and pliers to hold the nylon lock nuts while you tighten them into the 5/8-inch countersunk holes.

The strap acts as a stop, limiting how far the legs can open. Wrap one end of an upholstery strap around the middle of the top cross brace (D) and staple it in place with a narrow-crown stapler. Open the stool until the seat sits level, then pull the strap snug and staple the other end centered on the underside of the top step (A). Use several 1/2-in. staples at each end so the strap holds securely.

A step stool should be about 11 to 16-in. wide to fit both feet comfortably side by side. For a portable or compact version, stay toward the narrow end of that range.

A single-step stool should be 6 to 9-in. tall. That’s a good height for reaching into a truck bed, helping kids reach a tall bathroom sink, or getting to the top pantry shelves.

#7729. The Best Cordless Screwdrivers for Furniture Assembly, Repairs, and Tight Spots

Published Nov 5, 2026 11:47 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The right cordless screwdriver depends on the job. Compact models suit light household tasks, while more powerful ones handle dense wood.

An adjustable clutch helps prevent stripped or overdriven screws, especially on higher-torque models.

Cordless screwdrivers speed up furniture assembly, cabinet adjustments, and other jobs that require driving or removing a lot of screws. We tested 12 top models to see how each one performed.

A good cordless screwdriver should be comfortable to hold, easy to control, and powerful enough for the work you have in mind. Leading our lineup of top-rated screwdrivers is the Milwaukee M12 ¼-Inch Hex Screwdriver Kit. Its 15-position clutch offers precise control, while its 12-volt battery gives it the power to drive screws into tougher wood than the lighter-duty models can manage.

With so many types of cordless screwdrivers to choose from, the right choice also depends on where you’ll use it. For instance, a compact inline driver may be easier to maneuver inside furniture, while a pistol-grip model can provide more power. Ahead, we explain what to look for and how the tested models compare so you can choose the best cordless screwdriver for your projects.

To earn a spot in our lineup, a cordless screwdriver had to be easy to use, durable, and capable of everyday fastening tasks, with a battery that lasted through small projects. We drove screws into drywall, pine, and birch, and tested the new models in prefab holes, predrilled holes, and raw wood to see where each performed best. The picks below offer useful options for projects around your home or workshop.

Right out of the box, the first thing we noticed about the Milwaukee M12 was its weight. At just over 2 pounds with the battery installed, it’s heavier than many cordless screwdrivers, but it fits nicely in the palm and isn’t too cumbersome for installing multiple screws. It made quick work of inserting screws in drywall, and we were able to insert screws in both pine and birch boards as well.

The M12 is less about fancy features and more about getting the job done. This pistol-grip screwdriver uses Milwaukee’s 12-volt lithium-ion batteries to create a mighty peak torque of 175 inch-pounds. It has an RPM range of up to 500, which makes setting fasteners quick work. The 2401-22 model uses a ¼-inch quick-change keyless chuck to swap out bits quickly, and it features a 15-position clutch to help regulate torque. We were also able to switch into drill mode to cancel the clutch feature.

Get the Milwaukee cordless screwdriver at The Home Depot or Ace Hardware.

As soon as we slipped the charged 12-volt battery into the Bosch PS21-2A cordless screwdriver and pulled the trigger, we could tell it offered more torque than most. It has two speed ranges we were able to switch between by sliding a lever on the top of the tool. The screwdriver generates up to 1,300 RPM at top speed, which is quite an accomplishment for an automatic screwdriver.

It also packs some powerful torque, which meant we were able to insert screws with ease into drywall, pine, and birch boards. With that much torque, the 21-adjustment clutch is essential to prevent stripping out the screw heads.

In addition to ample torque and speed, this screwdriver is compact, with a head length of just more than 5.5 inches. It comes with two 12-volt batteries and a charger. Plus, there’s a built-in LED light to help users see in dim locations, but it would be better if it were brighter. If DIYers want a cordless screwdriver to tackle some heavy-duty jobs, the Bosch PS21-2A ought to do the trick. It’s a powerful tool in a small package, weighing just 1.4 pounds.

Get the Bosch cordless screwdriver at Amazon or Lowe’s.

If your goal is to find a budget-friendly, light-duty cordless power screwdriver that won’t crush screws, the Black+Decker 4V MAX cordless screwdriver may fit the bill. We were impressed by its versatile features and even more impressed by its budget-friendly price. While this tool doesn’t generate as much torque as some picks in our lineup, it still drove drywall screws quickly. It wasn’t as successful with wood, but that’s not what this tool is intended to do.

This screwdriver has a three-position handle that swaps easily from a straight screwdriver to a 45-degree or right-angle driver in seconds. It uses ¼-inch driver bits, so users can swap between bits or employ the chuck as a ¼-inch nut driver.

The screwdriver boasts an unusually bright LED flashlight, making it easy to see in dark areas. The 4-volt, battery-operated screwdriver comes with two bits and a charger. Its 4-volt lithium-ion battery held a charge well throughout the testing, and this model features a built-in battery and a simple charger cord that plugs in directly.

Get the Black+Decker cordless screwdriver at Amazon, Lowe’s, or The Home Depot.

For all those little household fastener chores, such as installing outlet and switch plates, tightening cabinet or drawer screws, or hanging pictures on a wall, we think this lightweight Makita cordless screwdriver set is just the ticket. At just 3.6 volts, this cordless screwdriver is designed for light-duty applications, and it excels at that.

Instead of requiring the user to remove a battery, the DF001DW has an internal battery that charges via a USB cord plugged into a computer’s USB port or a standard outlet using the included AC adapter. We tested the DF001DW by inserting and removing screws in drywall and wood. It comes with an ample 81-piece accessory set boasting bits for most types of screw fasteners used today, including Phillips, flathead, and star bit. Plus, the tool has an LED guide light that can be turned on when desired (it doesn’t stay on automatically when the screwdriver is in use).

The DF001DW also converts from a pistol grip to a straight-barrel grip, making it even more versatile. It weighs less than a pound, so it didn’t slow us down—yet it offered ample power for inserting and removing screws, even in wood, without the tool’s motor bogging down.

Get the Makita 3.6V cordless screwdriver at Amazon.

The Kobalt is a compact screwdriver best suited to the small fastening jobs that crop up around the house. We tested it on dozens of screws, including fasteners for prefab holes, predrilled holes, and raw wood. At just 0.49 pounds, it was easy to maneuver while assembling furniture, and the soft-grip handle made it comfortable to hold through a string of screws.

Its 280-RPM motor runs at one speed, so there’s no trigger control for easing a screw into place. It also lacks an adjustable clutch to limit torque. We found it most useful for driving screws into prepared holes, where its 13.5 inch-pounds of maximum torque are better matched to the task. For screws going directly into raw wood, especially as resistance increased, we’d reach for a more powerful driver. The built-in LED helps illuminate the screw head, and the charge indicator lets us check the battery before starting a project.

The kit comes with a range of bits, a magnetic bit holder, a case, and a USB-C charging cable. That makes it convenient to keep together for furniture assembly and quick repairs.

Get the Kobalt cordless screwdriver at Lowe’s.

Having previously believed the power to an outlet was shut off only to suffer painful shocks, we know the value of being able to test an outlet in a pinch. So we were pretty impressed with the Skil cordless screwdriver’s ability to sense if the outlet was still hot, just by depressing a button on the top of the tool. The Skil emitted a sharp warning beep when we tested a hot outlet, and a red light flashed. When we tested a dead outlet, there was neither a light nor a beep. This built-in safety feature is a boon for those who don’t typically carry electrical testers around while doing DIY projects.

This compact cordless screwdriver boasts a dual-LED light, 10 changeable bits, and a micro USB charger. The chuck accepts any ¼-inch drive bit and also functions as a ¼-inch nut driver. It has both forward and reverse, but no adjustable clutch or speed settings. While it inserted screws effortlessly into drywall, it bogged down when driving screws into wood boards. Still, it’s so good at sensing circuits that you could reserve this cordless screwdriver solely for electrical maintenance jobs.

Get the Skil cordless screwdriver at Amazon, Menards, or Acme Tools.

The Amazon Basics (formerly Denali) screwdriver doesn’t boast many bells and whistles, but it lets you choose from three torque settings. We found that handy when inserting screws into materials with different densities—for instance, more torque when inserting screws in wood than in softer drywall. It also features an LED guide light, but we found it to be dim and unlikely to offer much illumination in low-light situations.

The screwdriver charges via a USB-C cord (included). We liked this setup, as it simplifies charging—no need to remove and charge the battery separately. A compact tool measuring about 7 inches long, it was useful in restricted spots, but we would have liked a convertible grip. A barrel grip is excellent in some situations, but a convertible pistol grip would add versatility.

The only real downside we noted was that this model tended to bog down a little when we inserted screws in wood. It did the job, but it took longer than it did on drywall. Still, this is a handy little cordless screwdriver to have around the house or to keep in the trunk of a car for when small jobs arise.

Get the Amazon Basics cordless screwdriver at Amazon.

We tested 12 cordless screwdrivers from 10 brands, considering price, battery design, included accessories, grip, speed, torque control, and features such as work lights and interchangeable heads. We drove dozens of fasteners with each tool, using prefab holes, predrilled holes, and raw wood; earlier tests also included drywall, pine, and birch.

We noted how comfortably each screwdriver fit in the hand, how easily we could change bits and direction, and whether the screwdriver had enough power to seat screws without damaging their heads. After testing, we rated each model on a five-point scale for ease of use, build quality, performance, and value, using those scores and our hands-on notes to select the picks in this guide.

A slim cordless screwdriver can reach spots a drill can’t as easily. A cordless screwdriver drives screws faster than a manual screwdriver and reduces wrist strain by eliminating the need for repeated wrist motions. Its light weight and battery power also make it easy to carry from one task to the next. As you shop, consider where you’ll use it and how much power and control your projects require.

The more power a cordless screwdriver has, the faster it can turn. While cordless screwdrivers don’t require the amount of power that a drill driver or an impact driver might have, they still need enough juice to get the job done. If you’re purchasing a straight barrel-type driver, consider one with a speed between 300 and 500 RPM. This range is ideal for loosening or tightening a screw quickly without being too fast to handle. With pistol-grip models, speeds above 1,000 RPM are easier to control.

The more torque your screwdriver has, the denser the material that it can drive a fastener into. Heavy-duty screwdrivers provide more torque and may be suitable for driving a few drywall screws into wood studs, but this can drain the battery quickly.

Small cordless screwdrivers can reach and manipulate various types of screws into awkward spaces much more easily than a manual tool can. As long as there’s room for the tip of the driver to fit onto the fastener, you’re set—a powered screwdriver will help do the rest.

To fit into such tight places, the best cordless screwdrivers are highly maneuverable. A slim, compact design helps, and many models also have rotating handles that swap from a straight grip to a pistol grip, like those seen on drills and screw guns. Also, a smaller battery size makes cordless screwdrivers easier to tuck between boards and other low-clearance scenarios, such as behind sinks for plumbing tasks.

Many cordless screwdrivers come with rechargeable batteries, and they tend to range between 4 and 8 volts. Since a cordless screwdriver requires much less speed and power than a drill, these lower voltages are adequate. Two benefits of a smaller, lower-voltage battery? It fits in smaller places than full-size options, and it helps make the rechargeable screwdriver as light as possible.

Some lower-end screwdrivers use replaceable batteries. These models are less convenient and more expensive, since you have to replace batteries frequently. They usually have less power and torque as well.

If you have a large project coming up, it helps if a cordless screwdriver has enough power to see it through to the end. Luckily, battery life isn’t much of a concern for most of the best cordless screwdrivers because their small motors don’t use as much battery energy as a large motor does.

However, some cordless screwdrivers have a battery-level indicator that alerts users when the battery is running low. It’s helpful to know the battery status so that you can juice it up while on a lunch or supply-run break. Many models take about an hour to recharge.

Cordless screwdrivers tighten or loosen screws in prethreaded holes. They’re perfect for screws in electrical boxes and fixtures, screws used in automotive interiors and appliances, installing door locks and cabinet hardware, and other mechanical settings with threaded holes.

Except for the most heavy-duty electrical screwdrivers, these tools aren’t typically designed for lag screws and bolts, wood screws, or fasteners in other dense materials. While it’s technically possible to drive a screw through drywall with one of these tools, that’s simply not the type of job they’re made for. For this situation, grab a drill or an impact driver instead.

Cordless screwdrivers use toolless chucks, so swapping between bits is quick and easy. These chucks fit ¼-inch bits—the same bits used in standard multi-bit manual screwdrivers. There are also ¼-inch-drive drill bits, allowing a screwdriver to be used as a drill in light-duty material like thin wood or plastics.

The variety of ¼-inch bits available makes cordless screwdrivers incredibly useful: For instance, you can alternate from driving Phillips head screws to removing Allen or Torx screws in seconds. Most cordless screwdrivers use magnets to hold the bits in place while also providing a bit of magnetism to keep the screw on the end of the bit.

The clutch in fastening tools regulates the amount of torque applied to a fastener. Once the set torque is reached, the clutch will start to “slip,” preventing the tool from driving the fastener or drilling any deeper. Simply adjust the clutch according to the fastener and material type. Since this is situation-specific, the rule of thumb is to set the clutch to a low setting and increase slowly as needed.

Too much torque can break smaller, older, or low-quality fasteners. Fortunately, the best cordless screwdrivers have adjustable clutch settings to avoid stripping or breaking these fasteners. The clutch can also avoid overdriving the screw too deeply, which may also cause unwanted results.

Torque settings can make a significant difference when working with old, stubborn fasteners. Instead of tearing the heads off screws or stripping the fastener beyond recognition, the clutch will begin to slip, preventing the driver from continuing to turn and causing damage.

Not all cordless screwdrivers have adjustable clutches, though. Some don’t have the power to require one. However, higher-end screwdrivers with more torque usually do.

By the time a project with a lot of assembly is finished, your forearm and hand might be tired from using a manual screwdriver. Lesson learned: To forgo hand and arm fatigue, opt for a cordless screwdriver. This’ll also save you energy and time, allowing you to move on to the next project faster.

Being able to see what you’re doing is key to a quality finished project. If, while using a drill, the tool keeps getting in the way, it may slip off the screw, marring the surface or scratching the workpiece. Cordless screwdrivers let users see what they’re doing since a hand won’t block the view.

Instead of carrying several screwdrivers around in a tool box or tool belt, it can be easier to tote just one cordless model. Since the bits are easy to swap, a complete bit set can reduce the overall weight and free up space in a belt for other tools. It’s much easier to carry one cordless screwdriver with eight tips than eight separate screwdrivers.

A cordless screwdriver is a tool that many reach for again and again for a host of different tasks. Here are a few ways to get the most help from this handy tool.

There’s a lot to consider when choosing a new cordless screwdriver, so you may still have questions. If you’re still wondering about the ins and outs of cordless screwdrivers, check out these answers to some commonly asked questions.

A cordless screwdriver is a battery-powered tool that tightens and loosens screws with a motor and trigger rather than relying on hand power.

Cordless drills for DIYers accept several drill bit sizes with adjustable chucks, while mini cordless screwdrivers only accept ¼-inch bits. Also, cordless drills tend to be more adjustable in terms of speed, letting the user drill into different materials accurately and efficiently.

There are a few slightly different methods for operating a cordless screwdriver, but here is a general usage guideline:1. Choose the right bit and place it in the chuck.2. Adjust the direction you want to drive the screw (tighten or loosen) with the switch on the screwdriver.3. Seat the bit completely into the head of the screw.4. Maintain pressure on the fastener and squeeze the trigger.

Yes, higher voltage tends to be better for cordless tools, but there are some caveats. Cordless tools with higher voltages are certainly more powerful, but that power comes at a cost. They weigh more and are less compact than lower-voltage options. For cordless screwdrivers, 4 to 8 volts is usually sufficient, especially for light-duty tasks.

Yes, but it depends on how often you’ll use them and the tasks you do most often. They can save quite a bit of time and effort and can increase your efficiency, all at a typically affordable price.

#7728. A Ken Paxton Moment

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

As Texas AG, Paxton's done a lot of controversial and in-my-opinion unwise things, but this is the one that sticks in my craw

I have stayed away from discussing any of the many important electoral contests that will be (hopefully) decided today.  But given that he is at the center of one of the most hotly-contested Senate seats, I can't help being reminded of his conduct during the campaign to overturn the 2020 election results, and what may have been the lowest of many low points in Ken Paxton's career to date.

In December 2020, when he was Attorney General of Texas, Paxton was the attorney of record in a lawsuit against the states of Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, seeking to overturn the 2020 election results in those states.  He petitioned the Supreme Court to exercise its original jurisdiction to hear the case, and to do so on an expedited basis. [See my blog posting at the time here; Paxton's papers filed at SCOTUS are posted here].

Expert analysis using a commonly accepted statistical test raises serious questions as to the integrity of this election. The probability of former Vice President Biden winning the popular vote in the four Defendant States—Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin—independently given President Trump's early lead in those States as of 3 a.m. on November 4, 2020, is less than one in a quadrillion, or 1 in 1,000,000,000,000,000. For former Vice President Biden to win these four States collectively, the odds decrease to less than one in a quadrillion to the fourth power (i.e., 1 in 1,000,000,000,000,000^4).

The same less than one in a quadrillion statistical improbability [applies to] Mr. Biden winning the popular vote in the four Defendant States. . . . Again, the statistical improbability of Mr. Biden winning the popular vote in these four States collectively is 1 in 1,000,000,000,000,000.

Put simply, there is substantial reason to doubt the voting results in the Defendant States.

Indeed there is!  Prima facie proof of fraud in the counting of ballots, I'd say. But only, of course, it it's correct, or at least close to correct. But it's not correct.  It is, as anyone with a knowledge of elementary statistics would have recognized immediately, simply and laughably wrong. The technical term is, I believe, "utter bullshit." I explain why here.  The probability that Joe Biden would end up with a majority in any of those is not one in a quadrillion - let alone one in a quadrillion to the 4th power (!), which is approximately equal to the probability that the sun will rise in the West tomorrow, and will have developed the capacity for human speech - nor anything close to one in a quadrillion.

Hey, we all make mistakes, right? What is most disgraceful about this episode is not that Paxton screwed up in his brief to the Court; it is that he never acknowledges his error, either publicly or, more importantly perhaps, to the Court. His assertion that the probability that Biden actually carried these States was equal to the probability that you would pick the single blue marble from a collection of 1,000,000,000,000,000 marbles, is a falsehood, and it is one that is at the core of his argument, in a case that was of grave importance to the future of the country. If Paxton didn't catch that falsehood before he filed his papers with the Court, he's merely a lousy lawyer, which I suppose is nothing to get too worked up about, given that there always will be plenty of lousy lawyers out there. But if he doesn't acknowledge that he has misled the Court after those misstatements are revealed - if he doesn't tell the Court that it has to ignore the part of his argument that relied on this incorrect understanding of statistics - then he's in a much more sinister category.

That this is the candidate whom the Texas Republican party chose as its candidate for U.S. Senate speaks volumes about the current state of the Rule of Law in this Administration. I'm sure that Mr. Paxton is looking forward, assuming the results go his way, to forging a close working relationship with Attorney General Todd Blanche, who is similarly scrupulous in his adherence to fundamental Rule of Law principles (as in the Slush Fund fraud-on-the-court perpetrated by Blanche and the DOJ].

David Post is currently an Adjunct Scholar at the Cato Institute, and was previously a professor at Beasley School of Law at Temple University.

#7727. What Is “Heart Attack Snow,” and Why Is It So Dangerous?

Heavy, wet snow can turn an ordinary winter chore into a health risk. Learn why people call it heart attack snow and how to shovel safely.

Shoveling snow can be a dangerous winter chore. Icy walkways can cause serious falls, and prolonged exposure to the cold can lead to hypothermia or frostbite. Another safety concern is something called “heart attack snow.”

The name sounds dramatic, but it points to a real concern for people clearing sidewalks and driveways in winter. For those in snowy climates, understanding the risks of heart attack snow is important before picking up a shovel.

Understanding the risks can help prevent a routine chore from becoming a medical emergency.

Heart attack snow is a nickname for heavy, wet snow that’s harder to shovel than dry, powdery snow. The name comes from the strain that lifting this type of snow can place on the heart. According to the National Weather Service, snow with a higher water content weighs more, making each shovelful harder to lift.

The added effort can quickly raise heart rate and blood pressure. Cold temperatures also cause blood vessels to narrow, making the heart work harder. The American Heart Association warns that this combination can trigger a heart attack or sudden cardiac arrest.

The association says the risks are especially concerning for “people who already have cardiovascular risks like a sedentary lifestyle or obesity,” including those with a history of smoking, diabetes, high cholesterol, or high blood pressure. People who have previously suffered a heart attack or stroke also face greater risks.

Even lighter, powdery snow can be dangerous, especially when large amounts require repeated lifting or hours of clearing.

Before heading outside, people should warm up indoors and stretch gently. Dressing in layers helps protect against the cold, while staying hydrated is important even when someone doesn’t feel thirsty.

The American Heart Association recommends pushing snow rather than lifting it whenever possible. When lifting is necessary, smaller loads and frequent breaks can help limit physical strain. A snow blower can also reduce the amount of lifting, although operating one still requires effort.

Slippery surfaces are another concern. “Walking on ice is extremely dangerous,” according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The agency recommends using rock salt or another de-icing product to keep walkways clear of ice. Sand can also help prevent slipping.

People with heart disease or significant cardiovascular risk factors should have someone else handle snow removal, according to the American Heart Association.

Recognizing the warning signs of a heart attack is equally important. Chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, dizziness, nausea, cold sweats, or discomfort in the arms, back, or jaw can all signal a serious problem. Symptoms aren’t always severe and can vary from person to person.

Anyone experiencing possible heart attack symptoms should stop shoveling immediately and call 911. The American Heart Association advises against waiting to see whether symptoms go away.

American Heart Association, “Snow Shoveling, Cold Temperatures Combine for Perfect Storm of Heart Health Hazards” American Heart Association, “Warning Signs of a Heart Attack” National Weather Service, “Winter Weather Preparedness” Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, “Safety Guidelines: During & After a Winter Storm”

#7726. Yes, Different Curb Colors Have a Meaning — A Guide to Decoding Them

A painted curb can tell drivers where to park, stop, or unload. Here's what red, yellow, green, blue, and white curbs usually mean.

Finding a parking spot isn’t always as simple as pulling up to an empty space. Sometimes different curb colors come with their own parking rules, and drivers might not know what those colors mean. The different curb colors help drivers know where they can park, stop, or drop someone off.

The California Driver’s Handbook lists five common colors: red, white, yellow, green, and blue. But those colors don’t mean exactly the same thing everywhere. Cities have their own parking rules, and some areas have restrictions that only apply during certain hours. Los Angeles, for example, has different rules for loading zones, while Seattle uses yellow paint to mark some areas near driveways that drivers need to keep clear.

Learn what the five colors generally mean and what drivers should know before parking.

Red curbs generally mean drivers can’t stop or park there, even for a few minutes. That includes waiting in the car while someone runs into a store. They’re common near fire hydrants, intersections, and bus stops, where parked cars could block traffic or get in the way. Some red zones still allow buses to stop to pick up or drop off passengers.

White curbs usually allow drivers to stop long enough to pick up or drop off passengers. They’re often found outside hotels, schools, and hospitals.

But they aren’t regular parking spaces. Drivers generally need to stay with their vehicles and leave once their passengers get in or out. Some cities have different rules, though. San Francisco, for example, also allows certain white curbs to be used for quickly loading or unloading goods.

Yellow curbs usually mark loading zones. They’re often found near businesses where delivery drivers need somewhere to stop while dropping off packages or other goods. Commercial vehicles can typically use these areas for a short time, although some cities allow passenger vehicles to stop there, too. These aren’t regular parking spaces, and nearby signs usually explain how long drivers can stop.

Green curbs generally mean drivers can park, but only for a short time. They’re common near businesses where customers might need to stop for a few minutes. The time limit isn’t always the same, so drivers should check the curb or nearby signs before leaving their cars. Some spaces also have parking meters or restrictions during certain hours.

Blue curbs mark parking spaces for people with disabilities. Cities often place these spaces near building entrances to make them easier to access. Drivers need a valid disability parking placard or qualifying license plate to park in these spaces. Without one, they can’t use the spot, even for a quick stop.

The striped areas next to accessible parking spaces also need to stay clear so people have enough room to get in and out of their vehicles.

#7725. Court Orders Plaintiff to File Handwritten Opposition,

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

after noting that many of plaintiff's filings contained seeming AI hallucinations, despite assertions in plaintiff's filings that all the citations were valid.

From Judge Aileen Cannon (S.D. Fla.) in Paulk v. Larva Labs, LLC, decided in June but just posted on Westlaw:

This case presents a dispute over Defendant's alleged fraudulent interference with Plaintiff's Non-Fungible Tokens ("NFTs"). Plaintiff's Complaint, initially filed in Florida state court on January 20, 2026, alleges that in June 2017, Plaintiff used a publicly available software tool to generate 141 NFTs on the Ethereum blockchain. Each of these NFTs represents ownership of a unique CryptoPunk that was part of the first version of CryptoPunks ("V1"), a pioneering generative art project consisting of 24x24 pixel portraits. To create the NFTs, Plaintiff paid only nominal "gas fees" (i.e., fees paid to third parties who validate transactions on the Ethereum blockchain), and the NFTs "have remained in [a] dormant wallet" controlled to this day by Plaintiff.

Plaintiff alleges that, on June 23, 2017, Defendant "deployed" a second version of CryptoPunks ("V2"), "claiming V1 contained a 'bug.'" The Complaint then asserts that Defendant "suppressed V1 marketplace activity while promoting V2 as the sole authoritative collection, rendering Plaintiff's assets commercially impaired". Based on these allegations, the Complaint asserts causes of action for fraudulent concealment (Count I), unjust enrichment (Count II), declaratory relief (Count III), and injunctive relief (Count IV), seeking unspecified monetary damages and an injunction.

The court discussed various procedural issues, and then added:

As a separate matter, the Court is concerned more generally about the plethora of legal filings seemingly prepared by artificial intelligence and submitted by Plaintiff that make frivolous and unsupported arguments to the Court [see, e.g., ECF Nos. 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 26, 26-1, 31, 32, 33]. As an example, Plaintiff makes the obviously incorrect submission that the citizenship of Defendant's counsel can be considered in determining complete diversity.

And many of Plaintiff's filings contain disclaimers to the Court, expressly certifying "that every legal authority, statutory provision, rule of procedure, and historical case citation referenced within [the filings] has been independently read, analyzed, verified, and cross-referenced against official federal and state legal repositories." In each of these filings, "Plaintiff guarantees that every cited case stands as valid, binding law within the United States Supreme Court and the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals, possesses an active and unchecked standing, and accurately represents the procedural postures asserted." And he expressly warrants that he has not included any "fictitious or unverified citations," and that he has "manually double-checked" each case to ensure that it "support[s] Plaintiff's cause perfectly, ensuring that no unverified or 'hallucinated' data is presented to the Court."

No doubt Plaintiff's artificial intelligence legal counsel told him to say all this. And the AI certainly had the right idea—litigants should not make misrepresentations to the Court. Unfortunately, Plaintiff did not practice what his artificial counsel preached. Instead, he cites to "Snapper v. Redan, 523 U.S. 83 (1998)"—a case which does not exist—for the proposition that "when a company's chief legal representative has been sent formal notification at a publicly advertised professional office location, the entity cannot assert an administrative breakdown within its secondary commercial mail hubs as an equitable basis to vacate an otherwise valid default". Notwithstanding the made-up citation, the case Plaintiff means to cite, Snapper, Inc. v. Redan (11th Cir. 1999), is an Eleventh Circuit case that says nothing of the sort. Instead, Snapper established that federal appellate courts have jurisdiction to review remand orders based on the enforcement of contractual forum selection clauses. It does not mention vacatur, or default, or even mail—and it certainly does not stand for the extremely narrow proposition for which Plaintiff cites it.

In light of all this, Plaintiff has violated his duty of candor to the Court and has committed a Rule 11 violation…. [T]he Court [therefore] imposes filing sanctions as follows:

Plaintiff failed to respond to the motion to dismiss, and in a later opinion the court granted that motion.

#7724. What Does a Green Porch Light Mean? The Tradition, Explained
